transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-25
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~41 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samira Khan (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (CTO, Horizon), Evan Brooks (Lead Engineer), Riley Chen (DevOps)
Recording ID: ff-20260225-horizon-sdk-001

Summary (auto):
Quick SDK integration walkthrough covering Python + TypeScript examples, auth patterns (API key vs SSO/SSO token flow), environment setup, pointers to Redwood Console and Redwood Optimize suggestions, and next steps for POC. Action items and follow-ups captured.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Samira, AE on the Redwood team, with Luis, our SE. How are you all doing?
[00:06] Maya: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to see the SDK flow.
[00:10] Evan: Hi, yeah we want to see the path from SDK to production, auth story especially.
[00:14] Luis: Great. We'll run through the Python and TypeScript quickstarts, env setup, auth options, and then show the Console and Optimize quick hints.
[00:22] Riley: Sounds good, our infra questions are mostly around VPC/private deploy and KMS.
[00:26] Samira: Perfect. Quick qualification: are you leaning hosted API or Private/Dedicated?
[00:30] Maya: For initial POC hosted is fine, but enterprise will need VPC and customer-managed KMS long term.
[00:36] Evan: Also interested in latency targets — sub 200ms for short prompts and expected throughput of ~150 req/s for inference spikes.
[00:43] Luis: Noted. We'll capture that. For the SDK, we support two primary flows: API key (for hosted) and SSO/OIDC + short-lived tokens for private or stricter security.
[00:51] Samira: I'll share a quickstart repo that has both Python and TypeScript examples. link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/quickstarts/horizon-poc
[00:58] Evan: Nice. Can you run through the Python snippet?
[01:02] Luis: Sure. In Python it's a 3-line setup: pip install redwood-sdk, export REDWOOD_API_KEY, then client = Redwood(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')). Then client.chat.create with model and messages. Here's a sample: (reads) "from redwood import Redwood; client = Redwood(api_key=...); resp = client.chat.completions.create(model='redwood-8k', messages=[{'role':'user','content':'summarize txn logs'}])".
[01:38] Evan: Are there streaming examples? We want to stream token-by-token to our UI.
[01:42] Luis: Yes, both SDKs support streaming. In Python you can subscribe to a stream iterator; in TypeScript it's using the client.stream or EventSource pattern. We'll paste the snippet in the repo. Note: streaming over SSE tends to be most stable in browser environments.
[01:56] Riley: For TypeScript, do you provide both node and browser bundles?
[01:59] Luis: Yep. npm package supports node and has a small browser bundle for client-side embedding. We recommend server-side calls for sensitive prompts.
[02:06] Maya: About auth — we have SSO via Okta and a corporate KMS. How does Redwood integrate?
[02:12] Samira: Two parts: control plane auth (Console access) integrates with SAML/SSO for users; for runtime keys we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM on Private deployments. For hosted, we encrypt with our KMS but offer bring-your-own-key in Dedicated/Private. We'll share SOC2 and KMS docs.
[02:28] Evan: For hosted API with API keys, are there short-lived token options? We prefer ephemeral tokens from our auth service.
[02:34] Luis: Yes — you can mint short-lived tokens against your SSO or via our token exchange. Pattern: you authenticate your user/session, request a short-lived Redwood token, and use that on the client for a bounded time. We'll share an example flow in the quickstart.
[02:47] Maya: Great. Any rate limiting or quotas we should plan?
[02:50] Samira: We have per-key quotas and org-level rate limits. For spikes we suggest using Dedicated capacity or burst policies in the config. For the POC, we can provision soft higher limits while we validate.
[02:59] Evan: On the SDK side, what about batching? We have a worker that batches requests into multi-prompts.
[03:04] Luis: The runtime supports auto-batching on the server. SDK also exposes client-side batching helpers in the optimize module — e.g., Redwood.optimize.batchRequests([...]) — to bundle similar prompts to reduce cost. Note: batching trades off latency vs throughput, so for sub-200ms you may want smaller batches or dedicated capacity.
[03:22] Riley: You mentioned KV cache earlier in the docs — how does that work?
[03:25] Luis: The platform has prefix and KV cache to reuse model state across requests. We expose caching policies in Console under Redwood Optimize (sometimes the product name shows up as "Redwood Optima" in early docs — ignore that typo). Caching is great for repeated prefixes, but not useful for highly unique prompts.
[03:41] Evan: For private deployments, how does network flow look? Can we keep tokens inside the VPC?
[03:46] Samira: Yes. Private deployment keeps the runtime inside your VPC and you can configure internal auth endpoint. The control plane can be run as a customer-managed control plane in an air-gapped mode if needed.
[03:55] Maya: On instrumentation: can we get per-route latency and token-level cost breakdown?
[03:59] Luis: Absolutely — Console provides token-level cost, per-model latency histograms, and tracing hooks. We can also stream logs into your observability stack (Datadog/CloudWatch).
[04:09] Evan: Let's walk through a TypeScript quickstart.
[04:11] Luis: In TS it's similar: npm install @redwood/inference; set REDWOOD_API_KEY; const client = new RedwoodClient({apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY}); await client.chat.create({model: 'redwood-8k', messages}); For streaming in Node we use async iterators or EventSource in the browser.
[04:31] Evan: What about environment configuration? Any recommended env var names etc?
[04:34] Luis: We suggest REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_BASE_URL (for private deployments), and REDWOOD_ORG_ID for scoping. The quickstart has a .env.example.
[04:43] Riley: Are there SDK examples for automatic retries/backoff? We see transient 503s occasionally in other providers.
[04:49] Luis: SDK has built-in retry with exponential backoff and jitter; you can override retry policy in client config. We'll include recommended settings for 5xx and rate limit errors.
[04:59] Maya: For the POC we want to run a small benchmark — can Redwood run perf tests?
[05:02] Samira: Yes, Luis will help with a benchmark harness. We'll need a sample prompt set, target qps, and whether you need latency tail SLOs.
[05:11] Evan: We can provide a CSV of 500 representative prompts.
[05:14] Samira: Perfect. Action item noted.
[05:17] Luis: One more note on security: audit logs are available in Console and can be pushed to your SIEM. For encryption at rest with BYOK, the Private offering supports customer KMS; Dedicated supports limited BYOK via HSM integrations.
[05:33] Riley: Are there any gotchas with browser keys?
[05:35] Luis: Avoid issuing long-lived API keys to browsers. Use ephemeral tokens minted by your backend or token exchange. We'll include a sample token exchange flow in the repo.
[05:44] Maya: Anything about SDK versions and upgrades? We run pinned versions for stability.
[05:48] Samira: We follow semver and publish migration notes. Our Console can pin model versions and enforce model rollouts. We'll share the SDK changelog link.
[05:58] Evan: Cost controls — any suggestions to cap spend during POC?
[06:02] Luis: Set org-level quotas and per-key budgets. Also use Optimize suggestions for quantization or smaller model variants for non-critical paths.
[06:11] Samira: Ok let's recap next steps.
[06:14] Samira: I'll send the quickstart repo, Python and TS snippets, SOC2 and KMS docs, and a pricing estimate by Friday. Luis will run an initial throughput estimate and propose Dedicated vs hosted config for 150 req/s spikes. Evan will share prompt set and throughput targets. We'll schedule a POC kickoff next week.
[06:32] Maya: Sounds great. Thanks everyone.
[06:35] Riley: Thanks.
[06:36] Samira: Thanks all — we'll follow up in email with the links and action items.
